verses.text: Now these are the nations which Yahweh left, to test Israel by them, even as many as had not known all the wars of Canaan;
only that the generations of the children of Israel might know, to teach them war, at least those who knew nothing of it before:
the five lords of the Philistines, all the Canaanites, the Sidonians, and the Hivites who lived on Mount Lebanon, from Mount Baal Hermon to the entrance of Hamath.
They were left to test Israel by them, to know whether they would listen to Yahweh’s commandments, which he commanded their fathers by Moses.
The children of Israel lived among the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Amorites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites.
They took their daughters to be their wives, and gave their own daughters to their sons and served their gods.
The children of Israel did that which was evil in Yahweh’s sight, and forgot Yahweh their God, and served the Baals and the Asheroth.
Therefore Yahweh’s anger burned against Israel, and he sold them into the hand of Cushan Rishathaim king of Mesopotamia; and the children of Israel served Cushan Rishathaim eight years.
When the children of Israel cried to Yahweh, Yahweh raised up a savior to the children of Israel, who saved them, even Othniel the son of Kenaz, Caleb’s younger brother.
Yahweh’s Spirit came on him, and he judged Israel; and he went out to war, and Yahweh delivered Cushan Rishathaim king of Mesopotamia into his hand. His hand prevailed against Cushan Rishathaim.
The land had rest forty years, then Othniel the son of Kenaz died.
The children of Israel again did that which was evil in Yahweh’s sight, and Yahweh strengthened Eglon the king of Moab against Israel, because they had done that which was evil in Yahweh’s sight.
He gathered the children of Ammon and Amalek to himself; and he went and struck Israel, and they possessed the city of palm trees.
The children of Israel served Eglon the king of Moab eighteen years.

But when the children of Israel cried to Yahweh, Yahweh raised up a savior for them, Ehud the son of Gera, the Benjamite, a left-handed man. The children of Israel sent tribute by him to Eglon the king of Moab.
Ehud made himself a sword which had two edges, a cubit  in length; and he wore it under his clothing on his right thigh.
He offered the tribute to Eglon king of Moab. Now Eglon was a very fat man.
When he had finished offering the tribute, he sent away the people who carried the tribute.
But he himself turned back from the stone idols that were by Gilgal, and said, “I have a secret message for you, O king.” The king said, “Keep silence!” All who stood by him left him.
Ehud came to him; and he was sitting by himself alone in the cool upper room. Ehud said, “I have a message from God to you.” He arose out of his seat.
Ehud put out his left hand, and took the sword from his right thigh, and thrust it into his body:
and the handle also went in after the blade; and the fat closed on the blade, for he didn’t draw the sword out of his body; and it came out behind.
Then Ehud went out onto the porch, and shut the doors of the upper room on him, and locked them.
After he had gone, his servants came and saw that the doors of the upper room were locked. They said, “Surely he is covering his feet  in the upper room.”
They waited until they were ashamed; and behold, he didn’t open the doors of the upper room. Therefore they took the key and opened them, and behold, their lord had fallen down dead on the floor.
Ehud escaped while they waited, passed beyond the stone idols, and escaped to Seirah.
When he had come, he blew a trumpet in the hill country of Ephraim; and the children of Israel went down with him from the hill country, and he led them.

He said to them, “Follow me; for Yahweh has delivered your enemies the Moabites into your hand.” They followed him, and took the fords of the Jordan against the Moabites, and didn’t allow any man to pass over.
They struck at that time about ten thousand men of Moab, every strong man, and every man of valor. No man escaped.
So Moab was subdued that day under the hand of Israel. Then the land had rest eighty years.
After him was Shamgar the son of Anath, who struck six hundred men of the Philistines with an ox goad. He also saved Israel.

footnotes.content: The Lord leaves enemies in the land—not as punishment, but as a teacher. How easily we forget that the battle itself is part of His schooling, meant to keep us dependent on Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Children who never face hardship never learn true strength. God was raising a generation that knew war not from tales, but from their own hands learning obedience.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Five lords, multiple peoples—Lebanon to Hamath. The Philistines alone were formidable, but God left all of them. He teaches us not when the odds are even, but when they matter.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The test is always the same: will you listen? Moses gave the words; life makes the choice real. Our faithfulness now proves whether we truly heard the Lord yesterday.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They lived among the nations, not separate. Proximity without vigilance is its own kind of stumbling. We, too, are always one careless season away from drifting.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Intermarriage and idolatry arrive together—love opens the door that fear had locked. What we cherish softens the line between who we are and who we might become.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They forgot their God. Not all at once—there was a slow dimming, a forgetting of His name alongside a remembering of the gods around them. Evil often wears the mask of convenience.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yahweh's anger burned, yet He didn't abandon them—He sold them into servitude. Even judgment is a kind of faithfulness, a refusal to let His people harden into ruin.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When they cried out, He raised a savior. Not because they deserved it, but because crying out is itself a turning—an acknowledgment that they cannot save themselves. Othniel becomes the first of many.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yahweh's Spirit came upon him—this is not Othniel's cleverness or strength. The Lord Himself was the actual fighter, using a willing heart as His instrument.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Forty years of rest. A whole generation grew up knowing peace, and then Othniel himself passed into silence. Every rest ends; the question is always what we do with the quiet.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They fell again into evil, and the Lord strengthened their enemy. That word—strengthened—shows that even oppression comes from His hand. He does not simply watch us fail.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Eglon gathered Ammon and Amalek and took Jericho—the city of palm trees that once fell at a shout is now his stronghold. How quickly yesterday's miracle becomes today's loss when faithfulness fades.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Eighteen years under Moabite rule. That's a long season for a people to learn that independence from God tastes like tyranny by another's hand.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ehud was left-handed and a Benjamite—unusual in his weakness, unusual in his tribe. Often the Lord chooses the unexpected hand to do His work. They sent him to bring tribute, not knowing he brought deliverance.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A sword made by his own hand, hidden under his robe. What looks like cunning is really faith working with what he has—no grand army, just readiness and a heart trusting that the Lord will open a way.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Eglon was a very fat man—a detail as plain as it is particular. The writer sees the whole man, both his pride and his vulnerability. God often works through what we think we see clearly.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ehud sent the tribute-bearers away, clearing the room for what the Lord was about to do. Sometimes the stage must be emptied before the Lord's hand falls.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "I have a secret message." A true word carrying a false implication—Ehud speaks what the king wants to hear, then speaks the message the King of heaven sent. Obedience and faithfulness sometimes wear strange clothes.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Alone in the cool upper room—the king, stripped of his court, stands to receive what he cannot resist. Isolation and pride often walk together.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: His left hand drew the sword—the hand he was born with, the one he could trust. The Lord uses what men overlook: an unusual man with an unusual gift, delivering an unusual stroke.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The handle followed the blade; the fat closed on it. All resistance failed—the oppressor's own flesh sealed his end. Justice was certain and complete.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ehud departed calmly, locking the doors behind him. He did not flee in panic but walked out as one who knew the work was already done—a sign of a heart at rest in the Lord.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The servants saw locked doors and assumed modesty—covering one's feet was a euphemism for a natural need. They guarded his shame, not knowing it covered his death.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They waited and were ashamed, then opened the doors to find their lord dead. How often the Lord's deliverance arrives in the moment of our deepest doubt, and we see it only when we finally look.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ehud escaped to Seirah while the servants still hesitated. One man, one deed, and the tyrant's power dissolved like fog. The Lord had already won.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The trumpet sounded in the hill country of Ephraim—the signal gathered what one man alone could not. Ehud calls, and the people rise; what God begins, His people complete.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Follow me; Yahweh has delivered your enemies into your hand." Ehud speaks not as a general giving orders, but as a messenger announcing what the Lord had already done. The people move in the certainty of His word.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ten thousand Moabite men fell—every man of valor. The slaughter was total, decisive, the kind of rout that leaves no doubt who holds the field. The Lord does not settle for half measures.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Moab was subdued; the land had rest eighty years. Twice as long as after Othniel—a rest earned through a humbler, darker instrument. The Lord's ways reward faith, not cleverness or status.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Shamgar, a man we know almost nothing of, strikes down six hundred Philistines with an ox goad. Readers today hear an echo: the Lord uses what lies at hand, works through the nameless, and saves His people through the most unexpected means—reminding us that our smallness is no barrier to His purpose.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
